issue: Reconstructed gloss 'τὸ ἐκ βουλῆς αἱρετόν' presented inside quotation marks as Alexander's verbatim definition of prohairesis 'at De Fato 175'.
current:
Alexander defines prohairesis at De Fato 175 as: "impulse (ὁρμή) + desire (ὄρεξις) + what is chosen from deliberation (τὸ ἐκ βουλῆς αἱρετόν)."

PRO- (before) + HAIRESIS (choice) = deliberate choice, reasoned selection

From Aristotle NE III.2-3: prohairesis is wish + deliberation, the distinctive act of rational agency. It concerns means to ends that are IN OUR power.

For Alexander, prohairesis is the locus of genuine freedom. It combines:
1. HORMĒ - motivational impulse
2. OREXIS - desire for the good
3. BOULĒ - rational deliberation

Unlike Stoic synkatathesis (assent to impressions), prohairesis actively CHOOSES between alternatives, not just responds to external impressions.
proposed:
Alexander defines prohairesis at De Fato 12 (ed. Bruns) as the impulse, accompanied by desire, towards what has been preferred as a result of deliberation: ἡ ... ἐπὶ τὸ προκριθὲν ἐκ τῆς βουλῆς μετὰ ὀρέξεως ὁρμὴ προαίρεσις. In other words, choice combines impulse (ὁρμή), desire (ὄρεξις), and what is selected through deliberation (βουλή).

current:
σῴζουσα διδασκαλία (sōzousa didaskalia) - The teaching that saves; philosophy that preserves rather than destroys humanity.

Fat. 653-654: "Philosophy should save the human being, not destroy it. The saving teaching is this: that virtue and vice are up to us."
proposed:
The 'teaching that saves' — philosophy that preserves rather than destroys human agency (English paraphrase; no verbatim Greek is supplied because the phrase could not be sourced).

Alexander repeatedly tests doctrines by whether they 'save' (σῴζειν) the common preconceptions about what is up to us: e.g. De Fato 14 asks whether the Stoics, in saying all is fated, 'preserve the common preconceptions of all men about what is up to us' (σώζουσιν τὰς κοινὰς ... προλήψεις), and De Fato 31 turns the Stoic claim that determinism alone 'saves' divination against them. The doctrinal point — that genuine philosophy must safeguard, not abolish, that virtue and vice are up to us — is well grounded in these passages.

current:
**Avertissement conceptuel — anachronisme du « libre arbitre »** : la catégorie de « libre arbitre » (αὐτεξούσιον / liberum arbitrium) est, selon la thèse classique de Dihle 1982 — confirmée et nuancée par Bobzien 1998, Frede 2011, Fürst 2022 — une invention dogmatique chrétienne datant d'Origène (vers 230-250 ap. J.-C.). Les concepts anciens antérieurs — ἑκούσιον (volontaire) chez Aristote, ἐφ' ἡμῖν (ce qui dépend de nous) chez les Stoïciens et Académiques, voluntas libera chez Cicéron — recouvrent un champ conceptuel partiel et non-substitutif. Lorsque la présente description emploie « libre arbitre » / « free will » de manière apparemment naïve, il faut entendre une approximation lexicale moderne ; pour le contenu doctrinal exact de l'auteur ancien, voir le terme grec/latin propre. *(Phase 12)*

Christ's recapitulation as solution to human incapacity. Structure: (1) Problem: After the fall, humans "fell under the power of sin" (ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν πεπτωκότα). (2) Human INCAPACITY: "Those who could not save themselves" (τοὺς μὴ δυναμένους σῴζειν ἑαυτούς). (3) Paul proves "the weakness of man" (τὴν ἀσθένειαν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) via Rom 7:18, 24. (4) solution: Christ "recapitulates" (ἀνακεφαλαιόω) human history, accomplishing what humans cannot. (5) Salvation is "not by ourselves but by God's assistance." tension: Irenaeus affirms both free will (AH IV.37) AND human incapacity (AH III.20). Resolution: Free will for moral choices; incapacity for salvific self-rescue. More Pauline than other Apologists.

Christ's recapitulation as solution to human incapacity. The Greek original of Adversus Haereses Book III is not extant (the text survives in the ancient Latin translation), so the wording below is paraphrased, not quoted in Greek. Structure: (1) Problem: after the fall, humans have fallen under the power of sin. (2) Human incapacity: they are "those who could not save themselves" (Latin: qui salvare non poterant semetipsos). (3) Paul demonstrates the weakness of man via Rom 7:18, 24. (4) Solution: Christ "recapitulates" (the genuine Greek technical term is ἀνακεφαλαίωσις / ἀνακεφαλαιόομαι) human history, accomplishing what humans cannot. (5) Salvation is "not by ourselves but by God's assistance." Tension: Irenaeus affirms both free will (AH IV.37) AND human incapacity (AH III.20). Resolution: free will for moral choices; incapacity for salvific self-rescue. More Pauline than other Apologists.
